lesson.menu_desc: Disagreeing with elegance -- hedging and softened disagreement -- 30 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 13 -- I See It Differently
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rodrigo Marques de França | Lesson 13 -- I See It Differently

listenings.text: I have chaired arbitration tribunals for almost twenty years, and the most useful thing I ever learned was not about the law. It was about how to disagree with two very senior colleagues behind a closed door. When I started, I said exactly what I thought: that argument is wrong. It never worked. People defend a position harder when you attack it directly. So I changed the order. First I find the common ground, and I say it out loud. Then I name the one point I take issue with, and only one. And I use soft words for a hard point. I'd say the damages figure is a little high. I'm not entirely convinced by the second expert. The words are gentle, but nobody misunderstands them. A colleague once told me that I disagree more than anyone else on the tribunal, and that nobody ever notices. I took it as a compliment.

I teach negotiation to lawyers, and every year I see the same two mistakes. The first group is too direct. They say no, that's wrong, next point, and the room goes cold. Most of them learn quickly. The second group is harder to fix, because their problem looks like good manners. They hedge everything. Maybe, perhaps, I was just wondering whether possibly. After thirty seconds the other side has no idea what they actually think, and a lawyer who cannot be understood will not be taken seriously. So here is the rule I give them. One hedge per sentence, never three. Keep the point hard and the words soft. If you think a clause is unacceptable, you can say: I'm afraid we can't accept this clause as it stands. That is polite, and it is perfectly clear. Polite is not the same as vague.
